events_chronological: Between the wars, in a suburb outside the city, the novelist Vera Holt begins writing The Hostess while her husband Edmund and the servants manage her illness.
Vera's sister Nell visits with her children, and a dying bird is buried in the garden.
Vera tells Edmund at the railway station that she will die if she is kept in the suburb, and he agrees to move back to the city.
Vera decides that her heroine will live and that someone else - a poet - will die instead.
Years later Vera fills her coat pockets with stones and walks into the river, leaving a letter for Edmund.
In the post-war years, the pregnant housewife Hazel Fenn reads The Hostess in bed rather than get up for her husband Walter's birthday.
Hazel and her small son Robin fail at making a birthday cake and start it again from scratch.
Hazel's neighbour June comes to ask her to feed the dog while she goes into hospital, and Hazel kisses her.
Hazel leaves Robin with a sitter, takes a hotel room and lays out sleeping pills, and then decides to live.
Hazel comes home, gets through the birthday dinner, and leaves her family for good once the second baby is born.
In the present, Miriam Crest buys flowers for a party for her friend Gideon, a poet dying of an incurable illness who calls her by the name of the novel's heroine.
Miriam argues with Gideon, who will not be consoled and wants neither the party nor the prize.
Gideon's former lover Ansel visits, and Miriam breaks down in her kitchen over the summer they were all happy.
Miriam's daughter Fern and her partner Marnie watch her hold the whole day together.
Gideon tells Miriam he stayed alive for her, and lets go of the window ledge.
Hazel Fenn, now old, arrives from overseas for the wake and tells Miriam what she did and why.
Miriam lets Hazel stay the night, and Fern takes her upstairs.
Vera's letter to Edmund is read over all three women: to look life in the face, always, and to put it away.
nonlinear_category_reason: Three women's single days, each in a different decade, rotate as blocks matched on gesture and object rather than sequenced by date.
syuzhet_notes: Three days spread across most of a century are cut together as though they were one day, matched on gesture and object - a vase of flowers, a kiss at a kitchen door, an egg cracked in one decade and caught in another. Told-order bullet 1 is a prologue from years ahead of the material that immediately follows it, and the film uses no captions at all, so every jump between the three periods is carried by hair, furniture and light.
fabula_notes: The three strands are not causally simultaneous but are cut as if they were, so a single chronology pulls apart scenes the film deliberately fuses. The link between the housewife and the dying poet - that she is his mother, and that the boy of the middle period is the poet of the present - is withheld until near the end, and it is what makes this ordering legible at all.
